# Jeremy Lee for City College Board
中文網站
Donate
JEREMY • BUNNY • LEAH
Jeremy Lee is a third-generation San Franciscan, Asset Manager at Chinatown Community Development Center, and President of the Rose Pak Asian American Club, running for the San Francisco City College Board in 2026. His stated priorities include growing enrollment and class access, strengthening Cantonese and language access, protecting Free City and noncredit education, and supporting long-term financial stability.
This is the official campaign website of Jeremy Lee, a candidate for the San Francisco Community College District Board of Trustees, which governs City College of San Francisco (CCSF), in the November 3, 2026 election.
About Jeremy
City College Priorities
## 2026 San Francisco City College Board Election
San Francisco voters elect the seven members of the City College of San Francisco Board of Trustees, which governs the San Francisco Community College District. Jeremy Lee is a candidate for the Board in the November 2026 election. He is running alongside Dr. Bunny McFadden and Leah LaCroix as the Our City College slate. Read about Jeremy Lee, Dr. Bunny McFadden, and Leah LaCroix and their slate relationship.
Learn more about Dr. Bunny McFadden on her About page and Endorsements page. Visit Leah LaCroix’s campaign website for more information about her candidacy.
This site provides Jeremy Lee’s biography, City College priorities, endorsements, Chinese-language information, and campaign updates. Learn more about the CCSF Board of Trustees →
## Community Roots
Jeremy has worked for nearly a decade at Chinatown Community Development Center, with a focus on affordable housing, financial oversight, regulatory compliance, and community advocacy for immigrants, seniors, and SRO families. Both of his parents attended City College before going on to union jobs.
Read Jeremy Lee’s biography →
## Grow City College
Jeremy supports expanding high-demand classes, strengthening the pathway from noncredit to credit programs, and growing certificate and workforce programs. His approach links enrollment growth with the college’s long-term financial stability.
### Cantonese and Language Access
Jeremy supports strengthening Cantonese instruction at CCSF, protecting noncredit ESL, and making college information accessible to students and families in the languages they use.
Read Jeremy Lee’s City College priorities →

# City College of San Francisco Facts & Primary Sources
Last updated: October 11, 2026 · Published by: Jeremy Lee for City College Board 2026
CCSF’s most recent audited unrestricted operating result is positive, FY 2025–26 is reported as an approximately $18.4 million unaudited unrestricted operating surplus, and the FY 2026–27 adopted budget is balanced. At the same time, CCSF faces a future recurring-revenue challenge because its protected hold-harmless funding level does not automatically grow with cumulative statutory COLAs while operating costs can rise. Recent surpluses and future financial risk are not contradictory.
This page serves as the source-based hub for CCSF finances, enrollment and class demand, accreditation, Free City, Cantonese, and the 2026 Board election, with links to the underlying public records and deeper topic pages.
Relationship to Jeremy Lee’s City College priorities: Jeremy Lee’s published approach emphasizes enrollment growth, expanding high-demand classes, and long-term financial sustainability. This reference page assembles public financial records relevant to evaluating that approach. The records distinguish recent operating results from future projections; they do not independently establish whether any particular policy proposal will succeed.
Current as of October 2026: Based on the most recent audited actuals, CCSF is not operating at an unrestricted deficit. The most recent audited fiscal year shows a positive unrestricted operating result, and FY 2025–26 is also reported as an approximately $18.4 million unaudited operating surplus in the FY 2026–27 adopted budget. The current FY 2026–27 adopted budget is balanced and projects an approximately $288,000 unrestricted operating surplus. The same budget projects deficits beginning in FY 2027–28 under current assumptions.
## Explore CCSF topics
This page provides a concise overview. For deeper source-based guides on individual topics, see:
- 2026 San Francisco City College Board Election: Candidates, Issues & Differences — a neutral overview of the race, the two major slates, areas of agreement, and differences in financial and enrollment strategy.
- CCSF Budget, Surpluses & Reserves — recent operating results, projections, reserves, and long-term financial risk.
- CCSF Enrollment, Hold Harmless & Financial Sustainability — long-term enrollment trends, recent growth, waitlists, and course capacity.
- CCSF Accreditation & Governance — the 2024 warning, the 2025 reaffirmation, and the current accreditation status.
- Free City College: Facts & Sources — eligibility, tuition coverage, cash grants, and official program reports.
- CCSF Cantonese Program: Courses & Instructors — current Cantonese courses, schedules, and instructor listings.
## Does CCSF currently have an operating deficit?
Based on the most recent audited actuals, no. CCSF’s audited FY 2024–25 results show a positive unrestricted operating result of approximately $20.1 million. The FY 2026–27 adopted budget also reports an approximately $18.4 million unaudited operating surplus for FY 2025–26.
The current FY 2026–27 adopted budget is balanced and projects an approximately $288,000 unrestricted operating surplus. The same multi-year budget projects future unrestricted deficits beginning in FY 2027–28 under current assumptions. Those projections describe future risk; they do not change the fact that the most recent audited actuals show a positive operating result.
Primary source: CCSF FY 2026-27 Adopted Budget.
What budget is being discussed here? These operating-result comparisons do not refer to every District fund. CCSF’s FY 2026–27 budget identifies the Unrestricted General Fund framework—Funds 11, 15, and 39—as the core financial framework supporting daily operations. Restricted grants, bond funds, capital outlay, OPEB, financial aid, and other purpose-specific funds are accounted for separately.
## Common claims about CCSF finances: what do the records show?
Common claim | What the public records show | Primary source
CCSF is currently running a deficit. | The latest completed year, FY 2025–26, is reported as an approximately $18.4 million unaudited operating surplus. The adopted FY 2026–27 budget is balanced and projects an approximately $288,000 surplus, but the current year’s final actual result is not yet known. | CCSF FY 2026-27 Adopted Budget
CCSF has a structural deficit. | CCSF has projected future recurring gaps under current assumptions. That is different from an actual current operating deficit. | CCSF FY 2026-27 Adopted Budget
CCSF is running out of reserves. | The California State Auditor found that San Francisco Community College District’s reserves had grown substantially and were above the district’s then-current policy maximum. | California State Auditor, Report 2025-108
CCSF has no financial risk. | Future risk remains. The protected hold-harmless level does not automatically compound with cumulative statutory COLAs, while recurring costs can rise. CCSF therefore still needs to grow the amount generated under the regular Student Centered Funding Formula over time. | California Legislative Analyst’s Office, 2026-27 Community Colleges analysis
## Does City College of San Francisco have a structural deficit?
The phrase structural deficit is often used to describe a projected future gap between recurring revenue and recurring expenses. That is different from saying CCSF has actually ended recent fiscal years with operating deficits.
CCSF’s own financial materials show positive unrestricted operating results in recent completed fiscal years, while its multi-year forecasts also warn that future recurring expenses could outpace recurring revenue if enrollment and formula-generated state funding do not grow. Both statements can be true at the same time.
Key distinction: a projected deficit is a forecast. An actual surplus or deficit is what happened after the fiscal year closed.
CCSF’s FY 2026-27 adopted budget reports that the college closed FY 2025-26 with an $18.4 million operating surplus and an unrestricted ending fund balance of about $71.9 million. The same budget projects deficits beginning in FY 2027-28, while cautioning that those projections are not predetermined outcomes and will change as assumptions become actual results.
Primary sources: CCSF FY 2026-27 Adopted Budget; CCSF Final Budget archive.
## Has CCSF been running operating surpluses in recent years?
Yes. CCSF’s official budget tables show six consecutive positive unrestricted operating results from FY 2020-21 through FY 2025-26. The FY 2025-26 figure is reported as an unaudited actual in the FY 2026-27 adopted budget.
The exact figure depends on the accounting definition being used, so this page uses the college’s unrestricted operating result rather than mixing that measure with all-funds accounting, changes in net position, or other fund-balance measures.
Fiscal year | Unrestricted operating result | Status in CCSF source
2020-21 | +$7,758,172 | Actual
2021-22 | +$9,263,600 | Actual
2022-23 | +$5,632,730 | Actual
2023-24 | +$12,247,594 | Actual
2024-25 | +$20,119,638 | Actual
2025-26 | +$18,406,469 | Unaudited actual
Primary sources: CCSF FY 2023-24 Adopted Budget (FY 2020-21 and FY 2021-22 actuals); CCSF FY 2026-27 Adopted Budget (FY 2022-23 through FY 2025-26 operating results); CCSF Final Budget archive.
## What is the difference between a budget projection and an actual result?
A budget projection is based on assumptions about enrollment, state funding, cost-of-living adjustments, salaries, benefits, vacancies, utilities, and other costs. An actual result records what ultimately happened.
CCSF’s own forecasts have changed materially as assumptions became actuals. For FY 2024-25, CCSF’s adopted budget anticipated about a $1.6 million surplus, its mid-year revision increased that estimate to about $5.0 million, and the FY 2026-27 adopted budget later recorded an actual unrestricted operating surplus of about $20.1 million. Separately, the California State Auditor found that San Francisco Community College District ended FY 2024-25 with reserves roughly $20 million higher than it had budgeted.
That does not make multi-year forecasts useless. It means they should be presented as forecasts, not as completed losses.
Primary sources: CCSF FY 2024-25 Mid-Year Adjusted Budget; CCSF FY 2026-27 Adopted Budget; California State Auditor, Report 2025-108.
## What did the State Auditor report about CCSF’s reserves?
In its 2026 review of California community-college reserves, the California State Auditor found that San Francisco Community College District’s reserve increased over the audit period and was about 22% of general-fund expenditures at the end of FY 2024–25. That was more than twice CCSF’s then-current board-policy maximum of 9%, while remaining below the statewide median reserve of about 25%.
The State Auditor also concluded that CCSF had not adequately supported its 5% minimum and 9% maximum reserve thresholds with documented risk analysis.
Primary source: California State Auditor, “Some Community Colleges Have Growing Reserves but Lack Clear Spending Plans That Would Improve Student Outcomes,” Aug. 6, 2026.
## What did the State Auditor say about reserves above CCSF’s policy maximum?
Yes, with an important qualification. The Auditor found that San Francisco’s reserves substantially exceeded its existing board-approved maximum and that districts with funds beyond reasonable reserve needs could be missing opportunities to improve student and system outcomes.
At the same time, the Auditor also criticized CCSF’s old 9% maximum for lacking a documented risk analysis. In other words, the audit did not say 9% was necessarily the correct reserve level. For FY 2025-26, the Auditor calculated that applying CCSF’s existing policy would have produced a maximum reserve of roughly $25 million, while the district had budgeted nearly $58 million in reserves—about $33 million above that policy level. The broader recommendation was for a better-supported reserve policy, clearer disclosure, and a more deliberate plan for funds above actual reserve needs.
Primary source: California State Auditor, Report 2025-108.
## If CCSF has recent surpluses and large reserves, does that mean there is no future financial risk?
No. CCSF can have a strong current fund balance and still face a long-term recurring-revenue problem. The college’s future risk is tied in large part to whether the amount it generates under the regular Student Centered Funding Formula can eventually exceed its protected funding level while recurring costs continue to rise.
The protected floor itself does not automatically compound with cumulative statutory COLAs. However, the Legislature can provide separate increases that also apply to hold-harmless districts; in FY 2026–27, the state provided an additional 1.44% apportionment increase that applied to those districts as well.
This is why a complete description of CCSF’s finances should acknowledge both recent actual surpluses and the future challenge of growing recurring formula-generated revenue.
Primary sources: CCSF FY 2026–27 Adopted Budget; California Legislative Analyst’s Office, 2026–27 California Spending Plan: Higher Education.
## What is “hold harmless,” and how does CCSF move beyond it?
California’s Student Centered Funding Formula, or SCFF, determines community-college apportionment using enrollment, student demographics, and student-success measures. Hold harmless protects districts whose regular SCFF calculation is below a protected funding level.
CCSF’s FY 2026–27 adopted budget makes the current gap concrete: the college calculates approximately $156.4 million under SCFF before hold-harmless protection. An additional approximately $12.7 million in hold-harmless funding brings FY 2026–27 Total Computational Revenue to about $169.1 million.
CCSF moves beyond hold harmless when the amount it generates under the regular formula becomes greater than the protected amount. Spending reductions can lower expenses, but they do not by themselves increase CCSF’s regular SCFF calculation. Enrollment is the largest component of regular-credit SCFF funding, while supplemental and student-success factors also matter.
Primary sources: CCSF FY 2026–27 Adopted Budget; California Legislative Analyst’s Office — SCFF and hold harmless; California Legislative Analyst’s Office — FY 2026–27 apportionment increase. For the full causal mechanism, see CCSF Enrollment, Hold Harmless & Financial Sustainability.
## How does enrollment strategy distinguish the major 2026 CCSF candidate groupings?
All six candidates in the two prominent three-person groupings support enrollment growth. The difference in their published questionnaires is not “pro-enrollment versus anti-enrollment,” but the centrality and causal role they assign to enrollment in CCSF’s financial strategy.
Lee, LaCroix, and McFadden more consistently organize their published strategies around rebuilding the student base itself—course capacity, pathways, recruitment, retention, and barriers—while Ball, Lace, and Tam more often place enrollment within a broader institutional-management framework involving budgeting, reserves, facilities, program review, governance, and student outcomes.
This is a difference in emphasis and organizing theory, not a claim that Ball, Lace, or Tam do not understand enrollment’s financial importance. For the candidate-by-candidate analysis and direct links to all 19 publicly accessible questionnaires used in that comparison, see 2026 San Francisco City College Board Election: Candidates, Issues & Differences.
## Does CCSF have an enrollment problem?
Yes over the long term. CCSF experienced a large enrollment decline over the past decade and particularly during the pandemic. But long-term decline should not be confused with the direction of every recent semester.
CCSF reported a 10% increase in credit enrollment in Fall 2024 compared with Fall 2023, along with roughly 30% growth in new credit students. Recent growth does not erase the longer-term decline, but it shows enrollment is not simply moving in one direction.
Primary source: CCSF, “City College of San Francisco Starts New Academic Year with Increased Enrollment”.
## Is CCSF currently meeting student demand for classes?
Not in several high-demand subjects, according to published schedule and waitlist data cited by a CCSF instructor. In a 2026 San Francisco Chronicle Open Forum opinion essay, CCSF political science instructor Rick Baum reported that, as of August 14, all 48 Fall 2026 biology sections were full with 390 students on waitlists, and that chemistry offerings had declined from 58 sections in Fall 2019 to 17 in Fall 2026.
Baum also reported that all scheduled art classes had filled by early June and compared CCSF’s number of credit-class sections with several nearby community-college districts. These figures come from an opinion essay rather than independent Chronicle newsroom reporting, so they should be understood as the author’s analysis of public class schedules and waitlists.
This is an important distinction: lower institution-wide enrollment can coexist with full sections and waitlists in particular subjects.
Secondary reporting based on current CCSF class schedules and waitlists: San Francisco Chronicle, “City College is failing students by not offering enough classes,” 2026.
## Can CCSF grow enrollment if existing students cannot get the classes they need?
Course capacity can constrain enrollment growth in particular subjects. When a section is full, additional students cannot enroll in that section unless capacity is added or seats become available.
Because enrollment is a major component of the Student Centered Funding Formula, additional funded enrollment can increase the amount CCSF calculates under the regular SCFF and help narrow the gap between that formula amount and its hold-harmless funding floor. While CCSF remains below that floor, however, additional enrollment does not necessarily increase actual state apportionment dollar-for-dollar.
The 2026 Chronicle reporting on biology, chemistry, art, and English is therefore relevant to the financial discussion as well as the educational one.
Sources: San Francisco Chronicle, 2026 class-demand article; California Legislative Analyst’s Office on SCFF funding.
## What is CCSF’s current accreditation status?
CCSF is fully accredited. ACCJC placed the college on warning in January 2024 over financial decision-making and board-governance standards. In June 2025, ACCJC found that CCSF had corrected the identified deficiencies and reaffirmed accreditation. CCSF did not lose accreditation.
## Was the 2024 accreditation warning about widespread academic failure?
No. The warning concerned three standards related to financial decision-making and board governance. CCSF met 116 of 119 standards in the review. ACCJC later determined that the three deficiencies had been corrected.
Primary source: ACCJC follow-up report.
## San Francisco Republican Party recommendations in 2026 local races
For the November 2026 election, the San Francisco Republican Party lists Nicholas Berg as endorsed for District 2 Supervisor and recommends Alan Wong for District 4 Supervisor, Matt Dorsey for District 6 Supervisor, Laurence Lee, Phillip Kim, and Tim Tung for Board of Education, and Elijah Ball for Community College Board.
The SFGOP’s bylaws state that its political-affairs vice chair sends questionnaires to all candidates for local nonpartisan office and that a candidate who does not submit a completed, responsive questionnaire is not eligible for an SFGOP endorsement unless that requirement is waived by a two-thirds vote. The public November 2026 recommendation page, however, does not publish candidate questionnaires or identify which procedural steps each recommended candidate completed. For that reason, the public record reviewed here does not establish that every recommended candidate personally sought out or participated in the SFGOP endorsement process.
Two cases are more directly documented: Nicholas Berg is the SFGOP chair and received its formal endorsement for District 2 Supervisor. Phillip Kim received a formal SFGOP endorsement for Board of Education in the June 2026 election and is again listed as recommended for November.
As of October 5, 2026, no publicly available statement located in the candidates’ websites or current web coverage shows any of the candidates listed above rejecting, declining, or denouncing the SFGOP endorsement or recommendation. This is a statement about publicly verifiable information available as of that date, not about private communications.
Sources: San Francisco Republican Party — November 2026 endorsements and recommendations; San Francisco Republican Party — June 2026 endorsements; San Francisco Republican Party bylaws.
## Does fundraising establish which candidates have the strongest voter support?
No. A September 25, 2026 KALW overview of the City College Board race reported approximately $24,210 for Elijah Ball, $22,705 for Erwin Tam, and $16,380 for Monroe Lace. The San Francisco Ethics Commission reports the same Ball and Tam totals and $16,380.99 for Lace.
Those figures establish how much the campaign committees reported receiving; they do not establish how many voters support each candidate. Campaign-finance totals and voter-preference measurements are different kinds of data. KALW’s article does not cite polling of the CCSF race.
Sources: KALW — “Three seats, eight candidates: City College trustees face tough choices”; San Francisco Ethics Commission — Community College Board campaign-finance summary.
## How much of Erwin Tam’s fundraising came from his own money?
San Francisco Ethics Commission records show that Erwin Tam contributed $10,000 to his own campaign. Against the committee’s reported $22,705 in total contributions, that equals approximately 44.0%. That $10,000 is part of the committee’s contribution total but is not a contribution from another person.
Source: San Francisco Ethics Commission — Erwin Tam for Community College Board 2026.
## Does CCSF’s high share of spending on salaries and benefits violate an 85% state limit?
No. The 85% figure is an operational standard published by the Fiscal Crisis and Management Assistance Team (FCMAT), not a statutory ceiling that automatically puts a community college out of compliance when it is exceeded. FCMAT states that an average community college district should use no more than 85% of ongoing revenues for salaries and benefits so that at least 15% remains for supplies, materials, post-retirement obligations, capital outlay, and other operations.
California does have a separate statutory requirement commonly called the 50 Percent Law, which generally requires community college districts to spend at least half of the current expense of education on salaries and benefits of classroom instructors. That is a different rule and should not be conflated with the 85% FCMAT benchmark.
Primary sources: FCMAT Fiscal Alert for California Community Colleges; FCMAT Community Colleges Indicators of Risk; California Community Colleges Chancellor’s Office — Fifty Percent Law; CCSF Final Budget archive.
## Is Free City College a waste of taxpayer money?
“Waste” is a policy judgment, but the public record shows what the program does and how broadly it is used. Free City provides tuition-free access to eligible San Francisco residents regardless of age, income, prior degree status, or whether they attend full- or part-time. It supports transfer preparation, job training, upskilling, career advancement, and lifelong learning.
The City and CCSF’s 2022-23 Free City annual report says that more than two-thirds of CCSF’s credit-student population received Free City benefits that academic year.
Primary sources: CCSF Free City; City and County of San Francisco — Free City Annual Report 2022-23; City and County of San Francisco — 2019 Free City Annual Report.
## What exactly does Free City pay for?
Free City covers the $46-per-unit enrollment fee for eligible students. CCSF’s official Free City page states that it does not cover all other CCSF fees, including the health fee, web registration fee, student representation fee, student activity fee, and some course materials fees. A Free City recipient who also receives the California College Promise Grant is eligible for the Free City Grant at $46 per enrolled unit.
Primary sources: CCSF Free City; CCSF Free City Grant; CCSF Tuition and Fees.
## What Cantonese program does CCSF currently offer?
CCSF offers CHIN 10A, CHIN 10B, CHIN 10C, and CHIN 10D in conversational Cantonese. CCSF’s published Spring and Fall 2026 schedules list Grace Yu as the instructor for each of the four CHIN 10 sequence courses offered that year.
Primary sources: CCSF Chinese program page; Spring 2026 schedule; Fall 2026 schedule. See CCSF Cantonese Program: Courses & Certificate for the dedicated program page.
## Does closing or shrinking programs automatically solve CCSF’s financial problem?
Closing or shrinking programs can reduce expenditures, but spending reductions alone do not increase the regular SCFF calculation CCSF must eventually raise above its hold-harmless floor. Because the protected floor no longer receives future COLAs, staying at roughly the same formula-generated funding level while recurring costs rise can create increasing long-term pressure.
The fiscal question is therefore not simply whether CCSF can reduce spending. It is also whether budget decisions strengthen or weaken the college’s ability to attract, retain, and serve enough students to grow its regular formula funding. Cuts that reduce capacity in high-demand instruction or weaken enrollment pipelines can save money in the short term while making the transition off hold harmless harder.
Because enrollment is a major component of the Student Centered Funding Formula, restoring or expanding high-demand classes can increase access and can raise CCSF’s formula-calculated funding amount. For a district still receiving hold-harmless protection, that does not necessarily mean an immediate dollar-for-dollar increase in actual state apportionment; it can instead help close the gap between the regular SCFF calculation and the protected funding floor.
Primary sources: California Legislative Analyst’s Office; CCSF Five-Year Financial Projection.
## How should claims in endorsement guides be checked?
GrowSF’s 2026 voter guide is an endorsement document: it explicitly recommends candidates in the Community College Board race. Factual claims in an endorsement guide can be checked against the underlying budget, audit, accreditation letter, enrollment report, campaign filing, or state funding document.
For example, GrowSF’s 2026 voter guide notes CCSF’s long-term enrollment decline and the 2024 accreditation warning. It describes the college’s projected future recurring gaps as a “structural deficit,” while candidate Erwin Tam uses the phrase “fiscal cliff” for the risk created by a protected hold-harmless funding level. The primary-source record adds material context: CCSF’s recent actual unrestricted operating results have been positive, reserves have grown substantially, accreditation was reaffirmed in 2025, and the protected hold-harmless level creates a real future revenue challenge unless CCSF generates enough funding under the regular SCFF to exceed it.
Reference: GrowSF 2026 Voter Guide. Primary records: the CCSF, California State Auditor, ACCJC, LAO, and City sources linked throughout this page.
## What do the principal financial records show?
The source record establishes four separate points:
1. CCSF’s credit FTES remains materially below its 2018–19 level, although more recent years have shown some recovery.
2. CCSF’s recent unrestricted operating results have been positive; the FY 2026–27 adopted budget reports an approximately $18.4 million unaudited operating surplus for FY 2025–26 and an approximately $71.9 million unrestricted ending fund balance.
3. The California State Auditor calculated CCSF’s FY 2024–25 reserve at about 22% of general-fund expenditures, above CCSF’s then-current 9% policy maximum but below the statewide median of about 25%. The Auditor also found that CCSF’s FY 2024–25 actual reserve was about $20 million higher than budgeted.
4. Beginning in FY 2025–26, CCSF’s funding floor is based on its 2024–25 apportionment and does not receive future COLAs. CCSF receives the regular SCFF calculation or the protected floor, whichever is higher.
These records show both a strong recent fund balance and a future recurring-revenue challenge if CCSF’s regular SCFF calculation does not grow enough to exceed the protected floor while recurring costs rise.
